narrative.text: Lists the people involved in developing the guideline, beginning with the WHO Steering Group drawn from headquarters, regional and country offices. It continues with members of the other guideline groups and external reviewers from ministries, universities, cancer agencies and NGOs around the world. Each entry gives the person's unit or institution and location.

Recounts how the guideline arose from a 2010 decision to update WHO's 2006 guide to comprehensive cervical cancer control, and how the guideline groups developed PICO questions, outcomes and a modelling approach in 2011–2012. It notes that the guideline covers screening and treatment of precancerous lesions, not HPV vaccination, although the section title refers to managing conflicts of interest.

Thanks the guideline groups and McMaster University staff and students who worked on the systematic review. It names the main funders, the Flanders International Cooperation Agency, France's Institut National du Cancer and the GAVI Alliance, and the editing firm.
A list of acronyms and abbreviations used in the guideline, such as CIN, HPV, LEEP, VIA and GRADE.

Explains that untreated CIN2 or CIN3 lesions can progress to cervical cancer and describes the screen-and-treat approach, in which treatment follows soon after a positive screening test. It names the available screening tests (HPV test, VIA, cytology) and treatments (cryotherapy, LEEP, cold knife conization), and notes the guideline builds on earlier WHO guidance. It ends with research priorities and states that the recommendations apply to all women, with specific ones for women living with HIV.

Summarises the screen-and-treat recommendations, beginning with advice against cold knife conization so that all strategies use cryotherapy, or LEEP when cryotherapy is unsuitable. It sets out the panel's suggested preferences between strategies based on HPV testing, VIA and cytology with colposcopy, including options for resource-limited settings and countries with existing quality cytology programmes. The section also begins the background, describing how CIN is graded by the thickness of abnormal epithelium.

Introduces the goal of a screen-and-treat programme: reducing cervical cancer and deaths with few adverse events, linked to treatment and referral for invasive cancer. It explains how single tests and sequences of tests are used and how women with discordant results are managed. It notes that the recommendations rest on evidence about test accuracy and the benefits and harms of treatment.

Identifies the guideline's main audience as health policy-makers, managers and programme officers who choose cervical cancer prevention strategies, as well as reproductive health, STI, HIV and family planning staff.

Sets out what the guideline contains: screen-and-treat recommendations, a decision flowchart for choosing a strategy, and flowcharts for each strategy by HIV status. It also describes the methods used and points to online GRADE evidence profiles and evidence-to-recommendation tables.
A fragment stating that development followed the WHO handbook for guideline development.
Describes the three groups formed to develop the guideline: a 17-member Guideline Development Group, a 33-member External Review Group and a Methods Group from McMaster University.

Explains how the Guideline Development Group in 2011 narrowed 15 possible questions to eight through an online survey, dropping comparisons not used in practice. It then describes how outcomes such as cancer, mortality and treatment complications were ranked, with those rated important or higher included in the evidence review.

Explains that few randomized trials link screening strategies to treatment and patient outcomes, so the evidence came mostly from separate studies of test accuracy and of outcomes after treatment. It describes the systematic reviews, pooling of data and use of GRADE to rate evidence quality. It adds that evidence-to-recommendation tables were prepared summarising benefits, harms, values, resource use and feasibility.

Explains that the most accurate test is not necessarily the best choice, so a decision-analysis model was built to estimate downstream health outcomes of true and false screening results. The model calculated these for VIA, HPV testing and cytology, with assumptions set in advance and sensitivity analyses by HIV status and age.

Describes the April 2012 meeting at which the guideline groups reviewed evidence on benefits, harms, values, resources and feasibility to agree the recommendations. It notes qualitative evidence that women may fear screening and find a second visit burdensome. It explains how strong and conditional recommendations were distinguished, noting that many in this guideline are conditional.

Describes the review process, in which questions, review protocols, evidence and draft recommendations were circulated among the steering, development and external review groups before WHO clearance. It ends with a table explaining what strong and conditional recommendations mean for patients, clinicians and policy-makers.
Explains that a decision flowchart helps programme managers choose a screen-and-treat strategy, with strategy-specific flowcharts by HIV status in the annexes.

Sets out considerations that apply to all the recommendations, which target women aged 30 and over with priority for those aged 30–49, noting that even one screening in a lifetime is beneficial. It gives specific guidance for women living with HIV or of unknown status in high-prevalence areas, including screening once sexually active. It also covers screening intervals and follow-up one year after treatment.

Presents the detailed screen-and-treat recommendations, each with remarks, an evidence summary and the panel's reasoning. It begins with a strong recommendation against cold knife conization because its harms, such as major bleeding, outweigh a small reduction in recurrence. Later recommendations compare HPV testing, VIA and cytology followed by colposcopy, favouring HPV testing where resources permit and VIA over cytology-based strategies. The section ends by comparing sequential strategies, such as an HPV test followed by colposcopy or VIA; in the extracted text the evidence-quality ratings appear to be missing from the recommendation statements.

Notes the scarcity of randomized trials comparing screen-and-treat strategies on patient outcomes, especially for test sequences and for women living with HIV. It raises concerns about cytology programmes in weak health systems and discusses other factors such as loss to follow-up. It also mentions possible additional benefits of screening, such as detecting STIs, that studies do not consistently measure.

Describes plans to disseminate the guideline online, through WHO reproductive health channels and newsletters and in print to WHO's distribution lists. It mentions regional and country workshops to adapt the recommendations and notes that translations depend on funding.
Explains that downloads, country requests for technical assistance and changes to national recommendations will be used to evaluate the guideline.
States that new evidence will be monitored and the recommendations are expected to be updated about five years after publication.
A list of references for the guideline, citing mainly studies of HPV testing, cervical lesions in women with HIV and a WHO costing tool.

Discloses the declared interests of 15 of the 54 experts involved, such as conference travel support, research funding and industry links. Examples include support from EUROGIN for a speaker and PATH projects receiving donated vaccines and HPV tests from manufacturers. Each entry describes the nature of the interest in some detail.

Presents a decision-making flowchart to help programme managers choose a screen-and-treat strategy based on available resources, such as costs, staff and training. It notes that other factors, such as loss to follow-up with multi-test strategies, also need to be considered.
Introduces the flowcharts for each screen-and-treat strategy for women of negative or unknown HIV status, noting that they do not show which strategy is preferred.
A flowchart for screening with an HPV test and treating positives with cryotherapy, or LEEP if ineligible, with rescreening after at least five years for negatives.
A flowchart for screening with an HPV test followed by VIA, treating only women positive on both tests, with rescreening intervals for negative results.
A flowchart for screening with VIA and treating with cryotherapy or LEEP, with rescreening every three to five years.
A flowchart for screening with an HPV test followed by colposcopy, with or without biopsy, and treatment of CIN2+ lesions with cryotherapy or LEEP.
A flowchart for screening with cytology followed by colposcopy, with or without biopsy, and treatment with cryotherapy or LEEP.
Introduces the flowcharts for women living with HIV or of unknown status in areas of high HIV prevalence, noting that they do not indicate a preferred strategy.
A flowchart for screening women living with HIV with an HPV test and treating positives with cryotherapy or LEEP, with rescreening within three years.

A flowchart from WHO's guidelines on screening and treating precancerous cervical lesions for women living with HIV or of unknown status in high HIV areas, showing a strategy of HPV testing followed by VIA, with treatment by cryotherapy or LEEP only if both tests are positive.

A flowchart for the same group of women showing a VIA screen-and-treat strategy, with rescreening after negative results, cryotherapy or LEEP for positive results, follow-up at one year and referral if cancer is suspected.

A flowchart for women living with HIV or of unknown status showing HPV testing followed by colposcopy, with or without biopsy, and treatment by cryotherapy or LEEP, plus rescreening and referral steps.

A flowchart showing screening by cytology followed by colposcopy, with or without biopsy, and treatment by cryotherapy or LEEP for women living with HIV or of unknown status. It sets out rescreening intervals, post-treatment follow-up and referral when cancer is suspected.

Gives the literature search strategies used for the evidence reviews on diagnostic accuracy of HPV testing, VIA, cytology and colposcopy, listing MEDLINE search terms for cervical lesions and each test. It covers searches up to January 2012.

A PRISMA flow diagram showing how studies on screening tests and colposcopy were identified through database searches, screened and assessed for eligibility. It shows the numbers included in the meta-analysis, alongside an unpublished Cochrane review of HPV testing.

The reference list of studies included in the evidence reviews for the cervical cancer screening guidelines, citing mainly diagnostic accuracy studies of HPV testing, VIA, cytology and colposcopy from many countries. It ends with the publication's ISBN.

The front matter of the 2013 WHO guidelines for screening and treatment of precancerous lesions for cervical cancer prevention, with the cover, cataloguing and copyright page (ISBN 978 92 4 154869 4) and the table of contents. The contents also point to online supplemental GRADE evidence tables for women of negative or unknown HIV status and for women with HIV.
